newsitem.title: JAPAN: Too much paper choking Japan paper firm profits.
newsitem.headline: Too much paper choking Japan paper firm profits.

text.p: Japan's rocketing paper output may be too good to last after a personal computer boom last year had people poring over hefty instruction manuals and rushing to buy books and magazines to decipher them, analysts said.

"The outlook is not very bright," said Koichi Hariya, an analyst at Nikko Research Centre. "Demand for printing paper is easing, stockpiles are still swollen from last year's speculative demand and firms can't seem to coordinate production cuts."

Production hit a record high of 29.66 million tonnes in 1995, according to the Japan Paper Association. It attributed the rise partly to a brighter economy, but computer-related demand was what made paper mills whirl.

An average computer novice accounts for at least five kg (11 lbs) of paper, as a personal computer comes with at least two books of instructions, each weighing around 2.5 kg (5.5 lbs), according to association data.
And users generally need a pile of how-to books to decode the manuals and actually get the computer going, not to mention the mountains of magazines to keep up with the latest trends.
As a result, paper makers' profits as a whole quadrupled in the business year ended March 31, 1996. But this year, their profits are expected to crumble.
"It's partly because the paper companies raked in amazing profits last year," said Takashi Okatani, Wako Securities analyst. "The only way to go now is down."

Analysts said the biggest problem the industry is saddled with is huge stockpiles of leftover paper from last year because demand had not been as big as initially expected. But the worst is yet to come -- a glut of paper-making equipment.
"There's too much paper now and soon there will be too many paper-producing machines," Hariya said.
In 1997, four new machines with total annual capacity of about one million tonnes are due to come on stream, choking demand and profits still further.

Japan's largest paper manufacturer, New Oji Paper, reaped a profit of 48.07 billion yen ($437 million) in the year ended March 31, 1996. The company is due to merge with Honshu Paper Co Ltd in October to become the third-biggest paper producer in the world.

Daiwa Institute of Research sees New Oji's profit slipping to 42.5 billion yen ($386 million) in 1996/97 from the oversupply. With the glut expected to worsen next business year, its profits will plunge to 24.5 billion yen ($222 million), it said.

Current profits at Nippon Paper Industries, the industry leader in terms of sales, were 44.02 billion yen ($400 million) last year. However, Daiwa sees its current profit this year at 34 billion yen, and expects this to dwindle to 23 billion yen ($209 million) the following year.

Profits of the third largest company, Daishowa Paper Mfg, are expected to plummet to 11 billion yen ($100.0 million) in 1997/98, after rising 19.7 percent to 20 billion yen ($181 million) in 1996/97, Nikko said.

The previous glut in the late 1980s was caused by a capacity expansion of 2.7 million tonnes which sent many firms tumbling into the red. But this new capacity enabled paper output to hit a record last year, they said.
"If demand holds up, the industry may even see another tidal wave of profits before the century is out," Hariya said. ($1=110 yen)
